1. Sources, prerequisites, and the chapter contract

The four core courses are Oxford M1 Linear Algebra I (Andrew Wathen, 2022–23, native PDF pages 53–67), MIT 18.06SC (Gilbert Strang, Fall 2011, Sessions 3.6 and 3.7), Stanford EE263 (Stephen Boyd, Autumn 2007–08, Lecture 3, native pages 5–13), and Berkeley Math 54 (Alexander Paulin, Spring 2018, both four-page handouts on linear transformations and coordinate systems). Their contributions are complementary: Oxford supplies abstract proofs, MIT connects basis images to geometry, Stanford treats attainable outputs and coordinate ambiguity, and Berkeley derives directional coordinate matrices explicitly. CMU's written notes were also read and evaluated; specific errors make them an additional comparison rather than a core authority.

You should already be able to solve a linear system, recognize a basis, compute rank, and distinguish a vector space from an affine set. This chapter derives every new transformation theorem. The underlying field is denoted by F; unless another field is explicitly stated, numerical examples use real numbers. Matrices act on column coordinate vectors. Pn(F) means polynomials of degree at most n, including zero.

The target is reliable reasoning about linear maps, not memorization of a matrix identity without its input and output types. Every occurrence of a change-of-basis matrix below states its direction. Eigenvector bases and inner products appear only where they clarify this chapter; spectral theory and orthogonality have their own subsequent chapters. The selection is a documented comparison of accessible written courses, not a claim to have exhausted every course ever offered.

2. What linearity asserts

A map T:V→W between vector spaces over the same field is linear when

T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)

for every u,v∈V and every a,b∈F. This single statement is equivalent to additivity and scalar homogeneity separately. Set a=b=1 to obtain additivity; set b=0 to obtain homogeneity. Conversely apply additivity first and then homogeneity to each summand. Repeated application proves preservation of any finite linear combination:

T(∑j=1kajvj)=∑j=1kajT(vj).

Since T(0)=T(0+0)=T(0)+T(0), subtracting gives T(0)=0. Also T(−v)=−T(v). These are consequences, not substitute definitions. The map T(x,y)=(x,y2) fixes zero but violates homogeneity at (0,1) with scalar two. To disprove linearity it is enough to exhibit one valid failed combination. To prove it, checking only several sample vectors is insufficient.

The field matters. Complex conjugation satisfies addition and real scalar multiplication, so it is a linear map on the two-dimensional real space ℂ. It is not complex-linear: T(i)=−i, whereas iT(1)=i. Over a finite field even familiar polynomial formulas may behave differently; on F2, the scalar function x2 equals x. State the domain and field before declaring a formula nonlinear.

3. Linear, affine, and nonlinear geometry

A map x↦Ax+b is affine. It is linear precisely when b=0, because its value at zero is b. Affine maps preserve combinations whose coefficients sum to one. For example

T((1−t)x+ty)=(1−t)T(x)+tT(y).

A linear map preserves every linear combination; an affine translation preserves this restricted family. This explains why both can send lines to lines even though only the linear map must fix the origin. A singular linear map may collapse a line to a point. Thus “lines stay lines” needs a degeneracy qualification and does not characterize linearity.

Radially doubling every vector without changing its direction is T(v)=2v, despite the description T(r,θ)=(2r,θ) in polar coordinates. Polar pairs do not use componentwise vector addition. Testing linearity in that nonlinear coordinate chart would test the wrong operations. In contrast, replacing y by |y| folds the plane and fails additivity across the horizontal axis.

Both components scale together; this is the Cartesian form of radial doubling.

4. Basis images determine exactly one map

Let B=(b1,…,bn) be an ordered basis of V, and choose arbitrary w1,…,wn∈W. Define

T(∑j=1najbj)=∑j=1najwj.

This is well defined because the basis coefficients are unique. To prove linearity, write two inputs in that basis; the coefficients of au+bv are the corresponding linear combinations of their coefficients, so the displayed definition gives the required output combination. Any linear map sending each bj to wj must satisfy this formula, proving uniqueness. No independence of the output vectors is required. Dependence among the wj creates a kernel; it does not prevent existence.

For b1=(1,1) and b2=(2,1), suppose T(b1)=(1,0) and T(b2)=(0,1). The vector (5,3)=b1+2b2 has image (1,2). This is not obtained by treating (5,3) as the basis coefficients. In standard coordinates the input basis matrix is

P=(1211),A=P−1=(−121−1).

Indeed A(5,3)T=(1,2)T. Basis-image questions should begin by solving for coefficients, not by reading physical components as coefficients.

5. Prescribed dependent inputs and extension freedom

Suppose specified input vectors are the columns of X∈Fn×k, and their desired outputs are the columns of Y∈Fm×k. A matrix A satisfying AX=Y exists if and only if

kerX⊆kerY.

Necessity follows from Xc=0⇒Yc=AXc=0. For sufficiency define T(Xc)=Yc on the input span. If Xc=Xd, then c−d∈kerX, hence Yc=Yd; the definition is unambiguous and linear. Extend a basis of this span to a basis of the full domain and assign arbitrary images to the additional basis vectors.

If rankX=r, there are n−r independent unused input directions. Each can have any vector in an m -dimensional output space, so the solution set, when nonempty, is an affine space of dimension m(n−r). Over a finite field with q elements it has qm(n−r) members. If the specified inputs span the domain, existence implies uniqueness even if the list contains redundancy.

For inputs (1,0),(0,1),(1,1), the third output must equal the sum of the first two. Declaring three arbitrary outputs silently assumes independence that these inputs do not have.

6. Kernel, image, and fibers

The kernel and image are

kerT={v∈V:T(v)=0},imT={T(v):v∈V}.

They are subspaces: a combination of kernel vectors maps to zero; a combination of two attained outputs is attained by the corresponding input combination. For a specified y∈W, the fiber T−1({y}) is empty if y is not attained. If T(x0)=y, then

T−1({y})=x0+kerT.

Proof: T(x)=T(x0) is equivalent to T(x−x0)=0. Consequently all nonempty fibers have the same direction space and dimension, although a nonzero fiber is generally affine rather than a subspace. The zero fiber is the kernel.

The map T(x,y)=(x+y,0) has image the horizontal axis and kernel span{(1,−1)}. For output (3,0) every input is (3,0)+t(1,−1). Output (3,1) has no preimage. “Not injective” means multiple inputs produce the same attainable output; it does not mean every output is attainable.

An affine fiber parallel to the kernel

T(x,y) = (x + y, 0). Only outputs on the horizontal axis are attainable.

Adding a kernel vector changes the input without changing the attained output.

7. Rank–nullity with its proof

Assume dimV=n<∞. Start with a basis k1,…,ks of kerT and extend it by u1,…,ur to a basis of V. Every image is a combination of the T(uj) because the kernel basis images vanish. If ∑ajT(uj)=0, then ∑ajuj is in the kernel. Express it in the ki and use independence of the extended basis to force all aj=0. Thus the T(uj) form an image basis. Counting gives

dimV=dimkerT+dimimT.

This argument produces adapted bases rather than merely a number. In the domain order (u1,…,ur,k1,…,ks) and an output basis beginning with (T(u1),…,T(ur)), the matrix is the rectangular block containing Ir and zeros elsewhere. The kernel need not coincide with any standard coordinate axes; the normal form uses chosen bases.

For V of dimension n and W of dimension m, injectivity requires rank n and therefore n≤m. Surjectivity requires rank m and therefore m≤n. These inequalities are necessary, not sufficient for a particular map. When n=m<∞, either property forces the other.

8. Coordinate maps and typed representations

An ordered basis B gives a linear isomorphism κB:V→Fn, defined by κB(v)=[v]B, the unique coefficient column. Its inverse synthesizes the vector from those coefficients. If C=(c1,…,cm) is an output basis, the coordinate representation of T is

AC←B=κCTκB−1,[T(v)]C=AC←B[v]B.

Its j th column is [T(bj)]C, because [bj]B=ej. This derivation prevents two common errors: placing basis images in rows, and placing their standard coordinates in a matrix that promises C -coordinates.

If the spaces are ordinary coordinate spaces with basis matrices P=(b1…bn) and Q=(c1…cm), and A is the standard matrix, then

AC←B=Q−1AP.

The pipeline is input coefficients, physical input, physical output, output coefficients. Its operations are P, then A, then Q−1. Matrix composition is read from right to left. This formula requires both basis matrices to be square invertible; a redundant generating list is not a basis.

9. Full example with independent input and output bases

Let A=(1201), let B=((1,1),(0,1)), and let C=((1,0),(1,1)). Thus

P=(1011),Q=(1101),AP=(3211).

Multiplying by Q−1 gives

AC←B=(2111).

For input coefficients (2,−1)T, synthesis gives physical input (2,1)T, the physical output is (4,1)T, and output coefficients are (3,1)T. Applying the representation matrix directly to (2,−1)T gives the same (3,1)T. Checking both paths is a useful independent verification.

Neither AP alone nor Q−1A is the requested representation. The first retains standard output coordinates; the second retains standard input coordinates. The matrix Q−1AP is generally not similar to A, because two bases were independently chosen.

10. Directional change-of-coordinate matrices

For two bases B and D of the same space, define PB←D by

[v]B=PB←D[v]D.

Its columns are the vectors [dj]B. The inverse is PD←B, since converting in both directions recovers each coordinate column. For a third basis E,

PB←E=PB←DPD←E.

The middle labels must match. It is safer to derive this by substituting the two coordinate equations than to recall a word such as “transition matrix,” whose direction varies between textbooks.

With standard-basis matrices B0,D0, solve B0P=D0; equivalently P=B0−1D0. Augmenting [B0∣D0] and reducing the left block to identity computes the entire transition at once. Row reduction is a computational tool here; the pivot operations do not change the physical basis vectors being represented.

11. Composition and mismatched intermediate coordinates

Suppose T:U→V and S:V→W. If T uses output basis C and S uses that same basis as its input, then

[ST]D←B=[S]D←C[T]C←B.

If T outputs C -coordinates but S expects E -coordinates, insert the bridge:

[ST]D←B=[S]D←EPE←C[T]C←B.

Equal numerical dimensions do not make incompatible coordinate labels compatible. Associativity follows from substitution of functions; it does not permit reversing order. A horizontal shear H=(1101) and vertical shear K=(1011) satisfy

KH=(1112),HK=(2111).

Their images of e1 already differ: (1,1)T versus (2,1)T. A diagram should show the intermediate vector and named operation, not just two unrelated final shapes.

12. Inverses and one-sided recovery

A bijective linear map has a linear inverse. For yi=T(xi), linearity gives T(ax1+bx2)=ay1+by2. Apply the inverse to get T−1(ay1+by2)=aT−1(y1)+bT−1(y2). Its coordinate matrix reverses both the direction and bases:

[T−1]B←C=([T]C←B)−1.

A left inverse L with LT=IV exists in finite dimensions exactly when T is injective: necessity follows by applying L to T(v)=0; sufficiency defines L on an image basis and extends it to the codomain. A right inverse R with TR=IW exists exactly when T is surjective: choose a preimage for each output basis vector and extend linearly.

For a real full-column-rank matrix A, (ATA)−1AT is a left inverse. For real full-row-rank A, AT(AAT)−1 is a right inverse. Their existence does not make a rectangular matrix square invertible. Over ℂ, replace transpose by conjugate transpose in these Gram formulas. Over an arbitrary field, the stated Gram construction may fail even for independent columns; use the basis-extension proof instead.

13. Changing both bases and changing one operator basis

Let old input/output representations be A. Let P convert new input coordinates to old input coordinates and Q convert new output coordinates to old output coordinates. Substitution yields

Anew=Q−1AP.

This is matrix equivalence and preserves rank. When the map is an endomorphism and the same basis change is used at both ends, Q=P, giving similarity:

Anew=P−1AP.

Similarity preserves determinant, trace, characteristic polynomial, and the ranks of all polynomial expressions in the operator. Proofs: determinants multiply and cancel detP; cyclicity tr(XY)=tr(YX) follows by exchanging the two finite summation indices; and

tI−P−1AP=P−1(tI−A)P.

Taking determinants proves equality of characteristic polynomials. Multiplication repeatedly cancels adjacent PP−1, so f(P−1AP)=P−1f(A)P for every polynomial f. Independent input/output changes need not preserve trace, determinant, or eigenvalues, even for square matrices.

14. A passive coordinate change is not an active motion

An active transformation changes a physical vector while the axes remain fixed. A passive coordinate change keeps the physical vector fixed but changes its coefficient description. If v=P[v]B, changing the basis changes [v]B=P−1v rather than moving v.

Consider A=(213−2) and P=(1−2−25). Since detP=1,

P−1=(5221),P−1AP=(14−277−14).

The larger entries describe the same operator in a more skewed basis. The trace remains zero and the determinant remains −7. Equal trace and determinant in dimension two imply equal characteristic polynomials, but they do not generally prove similarity; scalar and nonzero nilpotent matrices can share characteristic polynomials without being similar.

15. Rotation, reflection, shear, and projection

A planar rotation through θ has matrix

Rθ=(cosθ−sinθsinθcosθ).

Derive its columns by rotating e1,e2. Angles add under composition. An animation of rotation must use Rtθ, not (1−t)I+tRθ: the latter usually changes lengths and can collapse the plane at a half-turn midpoint. A reflection across the line at angle θ has matrix

Fθ=(cos(2θ)sin(2θ)sin(2θ)−cos(2θ)).

It fixes the line direction, negates a perpendicular direction, and squares to identity. Its determinant is negative; no continuous path consisting solely of invertible real matrices connects identity to this reflection, because determinant would have to cross zero. A discrete reflection animation therefore explains the switch rather than pretending every intervening matrix is itself a reflection.

The shear (x,y)↦(x+sy,y) preserves area and horizontal lines but not angles. Orthogonal projection onto a unit direction u is uuT. A general projection is any operator P with P2=P; it need not be symmetric.

16. Oblique projections and complementary subspaces

If V=U⊕K, each vector has a unique expression u+k. Define P(u+k)=u. This is linear, has image U, kernel K, and satisfies P2=P. Conversely, if P2=P, then

v=Pv+(v−Pv),Pv∈imP,v−Pv∈kerP.

Their intersection is zero: if w=Px and Pw=0, idempotence also gives Pw=P2x=Px=w. Therefore every projection determines a direct sum. In an adapted basis its matrix is diag(Ir,0).

For projection onto the horizontal axis along span{(1,1)}, write (x,y)=(x−y,0)+(y,y), so

P=(1−100).

The discarded displacement is parallel to (1,1), not perpendicular to the horizontal axis. Its matrix is not symmetric, but its square equals itself. The complementary projection I−P has image kerP and kernel imP. For a real idempotent, trace equals rank, since an adapted basis has only zero and one diagonal entries.

17. Polynomial operators, characteristic, and evaluation

Differentiation D:Pn(F)→Pn−1(F) is linear. In monomial bases its j th degree column has the coefficient j one degree lower. Over characteristic zero, its kernel consists of constants and its image is all of Pn−1. For P2→P1,

[D]=(010002).

For a polynomial p=2−3x+4x2, multiplication by this matrix gives the coefficient column (−3,8)T, representing −3+8x. Inputs and outputs have different dimensions; treating this derivative matrix as a square operator changes the stated spaces.

In characteristic p, D(xp)=0. Thus the characteristic-zero kernel claim fails whenever that monomial lies in the domain. For P4(F2), the kernel is spanned by 1,x2,x4, and the image by 1,x2.

Evaluation at fixed nodes t0,…,tn maps a polynomial to its value column. In monomial coordinates its matrix has row i equal to (1,ti,…,tin). Distinct nodes give invertibility: a degree-at-most- n polynomial with n+1 roots is zero, so the kernel vanishes. Repeated nodes remove independent information unless derivative data are explicitly supplied.

18. Interpolation, dual measurements, and compression

For distinct nodes, Lagrange polynomials

ℓj(x)=∏i≠jx−titj−ti

satisfy ℓj(ti)=δij. They form a basis because evaluating a zero combination at node i extracts its coefficient. The evaluation matrix in this basis is identity, illustrating that a basis can be adapted to the measurement rather than to monomials.

An invertible synthesis matrix W gives coefficients c=W−1x. This conversion itself loses no information. Setting some coefficients to zero is a separate approximation step. With M a diagonal zero/one mask, reconstruction is

x^=WMW−1x.

This is a projection onto the retained basis span along the discarded basis span. It is orthogonal only for an orthogonal decomposition; arbitrary skewed bases produce oblique projections. The reconstruction error is x−x^=W(I−M)c. A nonlinear threshold rule that chooses a mask from the input is generally not a fixed linear operator, even though reconstruction for a fixed mask is linear.

A fixed mask deletes a basis component

This fixed mask projects onto the retained first basis direction.

This fixed mask projects onto the retained first basis direction.

19. Matrix spaces are legitimate vector domains

In Mm×n(F), fixing a matrix L makes X↦LX linear; fixing R makes X↦XR linear. The map X↦LXR is also linear in X. Allowing both factors to vary creates a bilinear operation, not a linear map on the joint pair.

Transpose is a linear map Mm×n→Mn×m. In the matrix-unit basis it permutes Eij into Eji. On square matrices over a field of characteristic not two, symmetric and skew-symmetric subspaces are complementary:

X=X+XT2+X−XT2.

The projection onto symmetric matrices has kernel the skew-symmetric matrices and rank n(n+1)/2. In characteristic two division by two is unavailable, and the displayed decomposition must not be imported.

Trace X↦trX is a linear functional. Its kernel has dimension n2−1 because it is surjective: tr(aE11)=a. Determinant is not linear for n≥2. The counterexample det(I+I) versus detI+detI works over the reals for most dimensions, but a field-independent disproof should use two diagonal rank-deficient matrices whose sum is identity for n=2.

20. Commutators and the Sylvester equation

For fixed A,B, the map L(X)=AX−XB is linear on matrix space. If A=diag(a1,…,am) and B=diag(b1,…,bn), then

L(Eij)=(ai−bj)Eij.

Thus its kernel dimension is the number of ordered pairs with ai=bj. The equation AX−XB=C is uniquely solvable precisely when no such pair exists; then xij=cij/(ai−bj). If a coefficient difference vanishes, the corresponding equation requires cij=0 and leaves xij free.

For a commutator AX−XA, every polynomial in A commutes with A, but that does not imply every commuting matrix is such a polynomial. When A is scalar, all matrices commute; polynomials in A span only scalar matrices. If A is diagonal with distinct diagonal entries, its commuting matrices are precisely diagonal matrices, and interpolation does express each as a polynomial in A.

21. Composition rank and precise preimage formulas

For T:U→V and S:V→W,

ker(ST)=T−1(kerS),im(ST)=S(imT).

Restrict S to imT. Its kernel is imT∩kerS. Applying rank–nullity on that restricted domain gives the exact formula

rank(ST)=rankT−dim(imT∩kerS).

Therefore rank cannot exceed either factor rank. Since dim(imT∩kerS)≤dimkerS=dimV−rankS, the Sylvester lower bound is

rank(ST)≥rankT+rankS−dimV.

Equality at the upper bound rank(ST)=rankT means S is injective on the attained output subspace of T, not necessarily on all of V. Full ranks alone are insufficient to identify a product rank without dimension and intersection data.

For maps S,T with a common domain and codomain, kerS∩kerT⊆ker(S+T) and im(S+T)⊆imS+imT. Equalities need not hold: T=−S makes the sum zero. In particular, ranks do not add mechanically.

22. Dual maps, transpose, and the adjoint boundary

A linear functional is a linear map to the scalar field. The dual map of T:V→W is T*:W*→V*, defined by T*(f)=f∘T. If A represents T in bases B,C, then AT represents the dual map in the corresponding dual bases. Indeed a coordinate functional row acts on A[v]B, so its coefficient column becomes AT[f]C*.

This is not permission to interpret AT as the original map on the original space. The direction changes and the objects are functionals. With real inner products, an adjoint T† can instead be represented on the vector spaces. If the Gram matrices of the input and output bases are GB,GC, then

[T†]B←C=GB−1ATGC.

Derivation: ⟨Ax,y⟩C=xTATGCy and ⟨x,By⟩B=xTGBBy. Equality for all columns forces GBB=ATGC. The simple transpose formula holds in orthonormal bases; complex inner products use conjugate transpose. This section establishes the boundary; full Gram–Schmidt and least-squares derivations belong to the orthogonality chapter.

23. Nilpotence, idempotence, and powers under coordinates

For an endomorphism, T2 means applying T twice with the same physical intermediate space. A nilpotent shift on Pn under differentiation has sufficiently high power zero in characteristic zero. On F3, the map (x,y,z)↦(0,x,y) has T3=0 but T2≠0. Its rank sequence is 3,2,1,0 for powers starting at zero.

Under similarity all powers are conjugated, so these ranks and the least positive zero power are invariant. Under independent domain/output basis changes, multiplying the displayed matrix by itself is usually invalid because its output coordinates differ from its input coordinates. To square such an endomorphism representation, insert the bridge from its output basis to its input basis.

An involution satisfies T2=I. Over characteristic not two,

v=v+Tv2+v−Tv2

decomposes the domain into the fixed and negated subspaces. This is why a reflection has a natural adapted basis. In characteristic two the two eigenvalue labels coincide, and a nonidentity involution can fail this direct-sum decomposition.

24. Infinite-dimensional counterexamples

Finite dimensionality is essential to the injective/surjective equivalence for endomorphisms. On all polynomials F[x], multiplication by x is injective but misses the constant polynomial one. On real polynomials differentiation is surjective because every polynomial has a polynomial antiderivative, but its kernel contains constants.

Represent polynomials by finite sequences of coefficients. The right shift R(a0,a1,…)=(0,a0,a1,…) and left shift L(a0,a1,…)=(a1,a2,…) satisfy LR=I but RL≠I: the latter erases the constant coefficient. This gives a concrete one-sided inverse counterexample outside finite dimensions.

Do not infer finite-dimensional identities from a formal infinite matrix without specifying its domain. Finite-support sequences, all sequences, convergent sequences, and square-summable sequences have different operator domains and additional analytic conditions.

25. A reliable solution procedure

First write the domain, codomain, field, and ordered bases. Second decide whether the problem asks about a physical map, coordinates of a vector, or a matrix representing a map. Third reconstruct missing basis images or identify their dependency constraints. Fourth compute kernel and image in one well-defined representation, translating a requested physical basis back through the synthesis matrix.

For a coordinate problem, draw the pipeline before multiplying. For a composition, match the middle basis labels. For a power, check that input and output coordinates agree. For a claim about uniqueness, check both attainability and kernel dimension. For a projection, verify the square identity and identify the two complementary subspaces.

Finally verify the result independently: test every basis vector, substitute a general parameterization into the original map, multiply claimed inverse matrices, or compute trace and determinant when similarity is asserted. A single numerical check is useful for catching errors but does not replace a universal proof.

26. Complete summary

A linear map preserves all scalar combinations over its stated field and is uniquely determined by images of a domain basis. Arbitrary prescriptions on a dependent list are feasible exactly when every input dependency is also an output dependency. A kernel records lost information; an image records attainable information; every nonempty output fiber is a translate of the kernel.

The rank–nullity proof builds a kernel basis, extends it to a domain basis, and maps the added vectors to an image basis. The coordinate equation is [T(v)]C=AC←B[v]B. Columns are output coordinates of domain basis images. General representation changes use Q−1AP; an endomorphism with the same basis at both ends uses P−1AP and preserves operator invariants.

Composition acts right to left and needs matching intermediate coordinates. Projections correspond exactly to complementary image/kernel decompositions. Polynomial and matrix-space operators obey the same theory once the spaces and bases are stated. The dual transpose acts on functionals in dual bases; an adjoint in nonorthonormal vector bases additionally contains Gram matrices. Finite-dimensional qualifications and field characteristic are part of the theorem, not optional footnotes.

Question 1. Explicit linear-map revisit: Dimension of symmetric trace-zero matrices

Authentic examination · checked English adaptation

MSc CS 1405 · Q41 · PDF page 9. Independently derived answer; not an official key.

Let W be the vector space of real symmetric 4×4 matrices whose trace is zero. What is dimW?

1.
10
2.
9
3.
8
4.
7
Read the complete solution and reasoning

Correct option: 2.

A symmetric four-by-four matrix is determined by four diagonal entries and six entries strictly above the diagonal. Thus the full symmetric space has dimension ten. Trace is a nonzero linear functional on this space: for example, its value on E11 is one. Its kernel therefore has dimension 10−1=9, giving option 2. To see the independence directly, use the six matrices Eij+Eji for i<j and the three matrices E11−E44,E22−E44,E33−E44. Their distinct off-diagonal and first three diagonal coordinates prove independence, and the trace condition forces the remaining diagonal coordinate. Option 1 omits the independent trace constraint. Options 3 and 4 incorrectly subtract further constraints; symmetry has already been included in the count of ten.

Question 2. Explicit linear-map revisit: An orthonormal basis defines a projection, not a norm expansion

Authentic examination · checked English adaptation

PhD CS 1404 · Q31 · PDF page 8. Independently derived answer; not an official key.

Let {u1,…,un} be an orthonormal basis of a subspace U⊆ℝm, with n≤m. Define Px=∑k=1n⟨x,uk⟩uk. Which statement is false?

1.

P is idempotent.

2.

If x∈U, then Px∈U.

3.

For every x∈ℝm, |x|2≤|Px|2.

4.

P is a linear operator from ℝm to U.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Correct option: 3.

Every image is a linear combination of the basis vectors, so it lies in U. Linearity follows from linearity of the real inner product in x. If x=∑akuk belongs to U, orthonormality gives ⟨x,uk⟩=ak, hence Px=x; in particular, P(Px)=Px. Moreover r=x−Px is orthogonal to every uk because ⟨r,uj⟩=⟨x,uj⟩−⟨x,uj⟩=0. The orthogonal decomposition gives |x|22=|Px|22+|r|22, so the universally valid inequality is |Px|2≤|x|2. The inequality in option 3 is not valid for arbitrary permitted subspaces: take U=span{(1,0)} and x=(0,1). Then Px=0 while |x|2=1. If U=ℝm, both norms agree; that special case does not establish option 3 as a general statement. The animation uses a two-dimensional orthogonal decomposition with labelled actual lengths, rather than pretending to draw arbitrary m dimensions.

Reduce each fixed factor to an identity/zero rank form using invertible changes. The induced changes on variable matrix coordinates are invertible, so map rank is unchanged. Only an r×s block of the transformed variable survives. Its independent entries give rank rs and nullity mn−rs. This is a matrix-space operator rank, not necessarily the rank of one particular output.

Question 40. A nonsingular Sylvester system

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original problem

Solve AX−XB=C for A=diag(1,3), B=diag(0,2), C=(2468).

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The entry multipliers ai−bj are 1,−1,3,1, all nonzero. Divide corresponding entries to obtain X=(2−428). Each equation independently checks (ai−bj)xij=cij. This is a four-dimensional linear operator with zero kernel, so the solution is unique. Dividing by A−B would not implement these four equations.

Solve independent matrix-unit equations

A diagonal Sylvester operator acts separately on each matrix-unit coordinate.

A diagonal Sylvester operator acts separately on each matrix-unit coordinate.

Step 1 of 2

(ai-bj)xij=cij

Question 41. A singular commutator system

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original problem

For A=B=diag(1,2), characterize all solvable AX−XA=C.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Diagonal multipliers vanish, so c11=c22=0 is necessary. Off-diagonal multipliers are minus one and plus one, giving x12=−c12 and x21=c21. Both diagonal entries of X are free. Thus rank and nullity are both two, and every attainable output has a two-dimensional affine solution fiber.

Zero multipliers create consistency conditions

The diagonal entries of the output must vanish; both input diagonal entries remain free.

The diagonal entries of the output must vanish; both input diagonal entries remain free.

Step 1 of 2

AX-XA=(0ab0)

Question 42. Commuting is not always polynomial

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original problem

For A=λI on M3(F), compare all commuting matrices with all polynomials in A.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

All nine-dimensional matrix space commutes with a scalar matrix. But every polynomial in it is scalar, spanning only a one-dimensional subspace. Therefore the valid inclusion of polynomials in the commutant is not generally equality. Additional structure, such as distinct diagonal entries, can change that conclusion.

Question 43. Exact composition rank

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original problem

T:F6→F5 has rank four. S:F5→F3 has rank three. The intersection of imT with kerS has dimension one. Find rank and nullity of ST.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Restrict S to the four-dimensional image of T. Its kernel has dimension one, so its image has dimension three. This is the composite image, giving rank three. The original domain is six-dimensional, so nullity is three. It is the intersection, rather than global kernel dimension alone, that measures how much attained information is lost.

Question 44. Positive factor ranks, zero product

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original problem

Construct two rank-one real 2×2 matrices whose product is zero.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Take T=diag(1,0) and S=diag(0,1). The image of T is exactly the kernel of S, so ST=0. Both have rank one. The exact rank formula gives 1−1=0, attaining the Sylvester lower bound 1+1−2=0.

An attained subspace is killed by the outer map

Each factor has rank one; their product has rank zero because image meets kernel.

Each factor has rank one; their product has rank zero because image meets kernel.

Step 1 of 2

T=diag(1,0)

Question 45. A product rank interval

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original problem

A is 8×6 of rank five and B is 6×7 of rank four. Bound rank of AB.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Rank is at most four. The intermediate dimension is six, so the lower bound is 5+4−6=3. Therefore only ranks three and four are possible. To decide, compute the intersection between the image of B and kernel of A. Using the outer dimensions eight or seven in the lower bound would be a type error.

Question 46. Cancellation enlarges a kernel

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original problem

Give S,T for which ker(S+T) is strictly larger than kerS∩kerT.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

On a nonzero real space take S=I and T=−I. Both kernels are zero, but the sum is zero with the entire domain as kernel. The intersection is always included in the sum kernel; cancellation prevents equality in general. The analogous equality for images fails in this example as well.

Question 47. Dual-map coefficients

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original problem

A=(120013). Apply its dual map to f(y)=4y1−y2.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Composition gives f(Ax)=4x1+7x2−3x3. Its coefficient column is (4,7,−3)T=AT(4,−1)T. The dual direction runs from output functionals to input functionals. The transpose acts in the corresponding dual bases, not as the original forward map.

Question 48. A Gram-corrected adjoint

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original problem

For Gram matrix G=diag(1,4) and A=(0100), find the real adjoint representation.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The formula is G−1ATG. Multiplying gives (001/40), rather than the ordinary transpose. For every x,y, equality of xTATGy with xTGBy verifies the result. Unequal basis lengths explain the correction; G=I would recover the transpose formula.

Question 49. Nilpotent rank sequence

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original problem

For T(x,y,z)=(0,x,y), find ranks of T,T2,T3 and its least zero power.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The matrix has ones at (2,1),(3,2) and zeros elsewhere. Squaring retains only position (3,1), and cubing gives zero. Thus ranks are two, one, zero, and the least positive zero power is three. This rank sequence is preserved by similarity because each power is conjugated by the same basis matrix.

A three-dimensional shift loses one layer per power

These are discrete applications; the ranks are two, one, and zero.

These are discrete applications; the ranks are two, one, and zero.

Step 1 of 4

T(x,y,z)=(0,x,y)

Question 50. Mixed-coordinate powers

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original problem

Identity has representation M=PC←B with distinct input/output bases. Derive its twofold-composition representation.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The first output is in C -coordinates while a second displayed application expects B -coordinates. Insert the bridge M−1. The correct product is MM−1M=M, not M2. The physical map is still identity after two applications. A numeric square is meaningful only for a representation whose intermediate coordinate types agree.

Question 51. Real involution decomposition

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original problem

Prove a real involution splits into fixed and negated subspaces.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

For T2=I, decompose v=(v+Tv)/2+(v−Tv)/2. Applying T fixes the first component and negates the second. If a vector lies in both spaces, it equals its own negative, so it is zero over the reals. Thus the decomposition is direct. Neither orthogonality nor symmetry is required.

Question 52. An involution in characteristic two

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original problem

Analyze A=(1101) over F2.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Squaring gives identity because the upper-right entry becomes two, which is zero. The matrix is not identity. Its fixed space is the first axis. Negated and fixed spaces coincide because minus one equals one. Their sum does not fill the plane, and the real half-sum decomposition is unavailable. This identifies the exact field hypothesis.

Question 53. An infinite-dimensional injective map

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original problem

Analyze multiplication by x on all real polynomials.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

If xp=0, coefficient comparison gives p=0, so it is injective. It cannot attain the constant one, so it is not surjective. This is an endomorphism of an infinite-dimensional space and does not contradict the finite-dimensional theorem. Each attainable polynomial with zero constant coefficient has a unique preimage.

Question 54. One-sided infinite shifts

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original problem

On finite-support sequences compute left-after-right and right-after-left shifts.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Inserting a leading zero then removing it recovers every input, so LR=I. Removing the first coordinate then inserting zero yields (0,a1,a2,…), which is not identity when a0≠0. Both operations preserve the stated domain and are linear. This is a valid one-sided inverse counterexample in infinite dimensions.

Question 55. Transforming kernel and image coordinates

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original problem

For M=Q−1AP with invertible P,Q, express its kernel and image.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The equation Mz=0 is equivalent to APz=0, hence kerM=P−1(kerA). Since P is onto, AP has the same image as A, so imM=Q−1(imA). Dimensions remain unchanged while the coordinate descriptions change. Translating a basis requires these same maps.

Question 56. Block form for an invariant subspace

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original problem

If the first r basis vectors span invariant U, which matrix block must vanish?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The first r input basis images lie in U, so their coordinates outside its first r positions are zero. Thus the bottom-left block vanishes and the representation is (AB0C). The top-right block may be nonzero because vectors in the complement may gain components in U. Invariance of both summands would force it to vanish too.

Question 57. The dimension of the map space

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original problem

Prove dimHom(Fn,Fm)=mn and construct a basis.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

For each (i,j) take the map sending input unit ej to output unit ei and other input units to zero. These maps have matrix units Eij. Any matrix is their combination with its entries as coefficients. Comparing each entry proves independence. Therefore there are mn basis maps, matching the freedom to select each of n images in an m -dimensional space.

Question 58. Trace of an idempotent

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original problem

Prove trace equals rank for a real idempotent and explain the finite-field limitation.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

An adapted image/kernel basis gives diag(Ir,0). Trace is invariant under similarity, so its real value is the integer rank r. In characteristic p its scalar value is r reduced modulo p and does not recover the integer rank. The image/kernel decomposition itself works over every field.

Question 59. Two measurements of a quadratic

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original problem

For T(p)=(p(0),p(1)) on P2(ℝ), find every polynomial mapping to (a,b).

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The matrix is (100111), rank two. The kernel is spanned by x−x2. A particular polynomial is a+(b−a)x. Every preimage is that polynomial plus t(x−x2). Two evaluations do not determine a quadratic uniquely; they leave one scalar freedom.

Question 60. An injective composite despite a noninjective outer map

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original problem

Can ST be injective when S:F5→F4 is not injective?

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Yes. Let T:F4→F5 append a zero fifth coordinate, and let S delete that coordinate. Then ST=I although S kills the fifth axis. The exact conditions are injectivity of T and zero intersection of its image with the kernel of S. Injectivity of S on the entire intermediate space is unnecessary.

Question 61. Polynomial identities survive similarity

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original problem

If A2−3A+2I=0 and B=P−1AP, prove the corresponding identity for B.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Adjacent inverse factors cancel, giving B2=P−1A2P, and I=P−1IP. Therefore B2−3B+2I=P−1(A2−3A+2I)P=0. This works for any polynomial. Independent domain/output changes generally do not preserve powers and must not be substituted here.

Question 62. Basis reordering at both ends

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original problem

Exchange the two basis vectors for A=(1234) and find the new endomorphism matrix.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The swap matrix is P=(0110), its own inverse. Conjugation yields PAP=(4321). Swapping only columns changes only the input basis; swapping only rows changes only the output basis. Coordinating both represents the same operator with a reordered common basis.

Question 75. Structured Sylvester classification 1

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original problem

For A=(1002), B=(0003) and C=(1234), classify AX−XB=C: rank, nullity, consistency and all constrained entries.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Each matrix unit Ejk has multiplier aj−bk. The difference table is (1−22−1), with 0 zero entries. Thus nullity is 0 and rank is 4. Nonzero differences fix x11=1, x12=−1, x21=32, x22=−4. It is consistent. The 0 zero-difference entries are free; every other entry is fixed above. The solution fiber has dimension 0. The ambient dimension is the number of variable entries. Substituting each fixed value into its scalar equation checks it independently.

28. Final examination rules and failure modes

Every rule below includes its hypotheses or an explicit boundary. Use this section after learning the proofs; it is not a replacement for the instruction above.

Linearity and specification

Rule 1

State the field before testing linearity. Complex conjugation preserves real combinations but fails complex homogeneity.

Rule 2

A linear map must send zero to zero. Passing that necessary check does not prove linearity; a square or absolute-value component can still fail.

Rule 3

Prove linearity for arbitrary inputs and scalars. Several successful numerical examples cannot establish the universal identity.

Rule 4

Disprove linearity with one valid counterexample. State both sides of the failed identity and verify that the chosen inputs lie in the domain.

Rule 5

An affine map Ax+b is linear precisely when b=0. Its preservation of weighted combinations with coefficient sum one is a different property.

Rule 6

Use the vector operations of the actual space. Componentwise addition of polar coordinates does not implement physical vector addition.

Rule 7

Radial multiplication by a fixed scalar is linear. A formula described using distances or angles can still be a matrix map after conversion to Cartesian coordinates.

Rule 8

Images of a domain basis can be chosen arbitrarily. Output dependence creates a kernel but does not prevent a well-defined extension.

Rule 9

Basis coefficients are unique, which proves that the extension definition is unambiguous. A spanning list without independence does not have this uniqueness.

Rule 10

A linear map agreeing with another on a spanning set agrees everywhere. The spanning set need not be independent for this uniqueness implication.

Rule 11

Prescriptions on a dependent input list must preserve every input relation. Test kerX⊆kerY for input and output column matrices.

Rule 12

If a dependent prescription violates one relation, no linear extension exists. Extra codomain dimensions cannot repair a specified contradictory relation.

Rule 13

If prescribed inputs have rank r in an n -dimensional domain, there are n−r unused basis directions. Each carries an arbitrary output vector.

Rule 14

A nonempty extension set into an m -dimensional codomain has affine dimension m(n−r). It is a vector space only when the prescribed outputs permit zero as an extension.

Rule 15

Over a field of q elements, that affine extension set has qm(n−r) maps. Counting formulas require finite field size as well as consistency.

Rule 16

Hom(Fn,Fm) has dimension mn. Matrix units and freely chosen basis images describe the same scalar freedoms.

Kernel, image, and dimension

Rule 17

The kernel is a subspace of the domain and the image is a subspace of the codomain. Keeping their ambient spaces separate prevents a dimension-type mistake.

Rule 18

A fiber outside the image is empty. A nonempty fiber is x0+kerT, not generally the kernel itself.

Rule 19

The fiber of a nonzero attainable output is never a vector subspace, because it cannot contain the zero input. Describe it as a translate of the kernel.

Rule 20

Every nonempty fiber has the same direction space and dimension. The position depends on the selected output and particular preimage.

Rule 21

Injectivity is equivalent to a zero kernel. Apply linearity to T(u)=T(v) to reduce it to u−v∈kerT.

Rule 22

Surjectivity is equivalent to image equal to the codomain. It concerns attainable outputs, not the uniqueness of inputs.

Rule 23

Rank–nullity uses the dimension of the domain. Subtracting rank from codomain dimension gives a cokernel count, not nullity.

Rule 24

The rank–nullity proof extends a kernel basis. Images of the added basis vectors are independent and span the image.

Rule 25

A map from dimension n to dimension m can be injective only if n≤m. This inequality is necessary and does not force a particular map to be injective.

Rule 26

Such a map can be onto only if m≤n. Equal dimensions make injectivity and surjectivity equivalent only in finite dimensions.

Rule 27

An adapted input/output basis puts a rank- r map into rectangular identity/zero form. This generally requires independent changes at the two ends.

Rule 28

Standard-coordinate kernel directions need not align with coordinate axes. Do not draw a rank collapse as deleting specific original coordinates without justification.

Coordinates, composition, and inverses

Rule 29

An ordered basis gives a coefficient isomorphism. The physical vector and its coefficient column are different typed objects, even when both are written as tuples.

Rule 30

A representation matrix maps input-basis coefficients to output-basis coefficients. Write [T(v)]C=AC←B[v]B before computing.

Rule 31

Column j contains [T(bj)]C. Rows contain output-component functionals; they are not the basis images themselves.

Rule 32

With physical standard matrix A and synthesis matrices P,Q, the representation is Q−1AP. Read the operations from right to left.

Rule 33

AP retains standard output coordinates. Q−1A retains standard input coordinates; neither is the two-basis representation by itself.

Rule 34

A basis matrix is square invertible. A rectangular or dependent generator matrix cannot be inverted as a coordinate isomorphism.

Rule 35

PB←D converts D -coefficients to B -coefficients. Its columns are D basis vectors expressed in B.

Rule 36

The inverse transition reverses direction. A phrase such as “from the old basis to the new basis” is ambiguous until its coordinate equation is stated.

Rule 37

Coordinate transitions compose with matching middle labels. Derive PB←E=PB←DPD←E by substitution.

Rule 38

For a transition computed from standard synthesis matrices, solve B0P=D0. Reducing [B0∣D0] computes all columns together.

Rule 39

Passive coordinate conversion keeps the physical vector fixed. Active transformation changes the physical vector under a fixed coordinate system.

Rule 40

A composite ST applies T first. The representation order is [S][T] when intermediate bases agree.

Rule 41

If the intermediate bases differ, insert their directional transition between the two matrices. Numeric dimension compatibility cannot detect this omission.

Rule 42

Associativity allows regrouping but never reverses factors. A two-vector shear example can expose a mistaken order immediately.

Rule 43

A bijective linear map has a linear inverse. Its inverse representation reverses both physical direction and input/output basis labels.

Rule 44

A left inverse implies injectivity. A right inverse implies surjectivity; they are different claims for rectangular maps.

Rule 45

In finite dimensions an injection admits a left inverse by extending an image basis. A surjection admits a right inverse by choosing basis-vector preimages.

Rule 46

A real full-column-rank matrix has Gram left inverse (ATA)−1AT. Over complex scalars use conjugate transpose.

Rule 47

A real full-row-rank matrix has Gram right inverse AT(AAT)−1. Over a general field the Gram construction may fail, so use basis arguments.

Rule 48

A one-sided inverse becomes two-sided for square finite-dimensional maps. Infinite-dimensional shifts provide a counterexample to dropping the finiteness condition.

Equivalence, similarity, and geometry

Rule 49

Independent changes at the two ends give Q−1AP and preserve rank. They do not generally preserve trace, determinant, or eigenvalues.

Rule 50

The same basis change for an endomorphism gives P−1AP. This is similarity and preserves operator structure.

Rule 51

Similarity preserves determinant by multiplicative cancellation. Verify the determinant of the basis matrix is nonzero before invoking it.

Rule 52

Similarity preserves trace by cyclicity. Equal trace and determinant alone are not a general similarity test.

Rule 53

Similarity preserves characteristic polynomial. A zero matrix and a nonzero nilpotent matrix can share that polynomial and still have different ranks.

Rule 54

Polynomial identities and ranks of powers survive similarity. Repeated cancellation gives f(P−1AP)=P−1f(A)P.

Rule 55

Powers require a common input/output basis. A mixed-basis endomorphism representation needs a coordinate bridge before another application.

Rule 56

A rotation matrix is derived from the rotated coordinate units. To animate rotation, vary the angle rather than interpolate arbitrary matrix entries.

Rule 57

Interpolating identity and a half-turn linearly collapses the plane at the midpoint. That family is not a sequence of rotations.

Rule 58

A reflection squares to identity and reverses orientation. An invertible continuous real path from identity to a reflection cannot avoid a zero determinant.

Rule 59

A shear can preserve area without preserving angles or lengths. Determinant one is not an orthogonality condition.

Rule 60

A projection is characterized by P2=P. Symmetry is an additional requirement for Euclidean orthogonal projection.

Rule 61

Every projection splits the domain into image and kernel. The retained and discarded directions need not be perpendicular.

Rule 62

I−P is the complementary projection. Its image is kerP and its kernel is imP.

Rule 63

Commuting projections have an idempotent product. Without commutation their product can fail the projection identity.

Rule 64

Over the reals an idempotent has trace equal to rank. In positive characteristic the trace scalar records that integer only modulo the characteristic.

Function and matrix-space operators

Rule 65

Differentiation is linear once its polynomial spaces are stated. Pn→Pn−1 has different input and output dimensions.

Rule 66

In characteristic zero the derivative kernel on Pn is the constants. Positive characteristic can create additional zero derivatives such as xp.

Rule 67

Evaluation at fixed nodes is a linear measurement. Distinct nodes and a degree bound determine when enough measurements give uniqueness.

Rule 68

Repeated evaluation at the same node is redundant. Derivative measurements at that node are different information and must be explicitly specified.

Rule 69

Lagrange polynomials form an evaluation-adapted basis. In that basis the full distinct-node evaluation matrix is identity.

Rule 70

Invertible basis conversion loses no information. Discarding coefficients is a separate approximation step.

Rule 71

A fixed zero/one coefficient mask reconstructs a projection. An input-dependent threshold generally makes the overall rule nonlinear.

Rule 72

Fixed left/right matrix multiplication is linear in the variable matrix. Jointly varying both factors gives a bilinear operation rather than a joint linear map.

Rule 73

The rank of X↦AX is nrankA when X has n columns. Count independent column copies.

Rule 74

The rank of X↦AXB is rankArankB. Use rank-form coordinate changes to justify the entry count.

Rule 75

Transpose is linear on matrix space and permutes matrix units. It is not automatically the coordinate-free adjoint of an unrelated operator.

Rule 76

Trace is a linear functional and remains nonzero in every field. The trace of identity can vanish in positive characteristic without making the whole functional zero.

Rule 77

Determinant is not a linear functional in dimension at least two. Two singular diagonal summands whose sum is identity provide a clean counterexample in dimension two.

Rule 78

For diagonal Sylvester factors, each matrix unit has multiplier ai−bj. Zero multipliers create both output consistency conditions and free input entries.

Rule 79

The commutant contains all polynomials in the fixed matrix. Equality fails for a scalar matrix, where every matrix commutes.

Rule 80

Composite rank equals rankT−dim(imT∩kerS). The intersection is taken in the intermediate space.

Rule 81

The Sylvester product lower bound subtracts intermediate dimension. Factor ranks alone may leave several possible product ranks.

Rule 82

Kernel intersections are contained in the kernel of a sum, but cancellation prevents equality in general. Likewise images of sums need not equal sums of images.

Rule 83

A dual map acts on functionals in the reverse direction and has transpose matrix in dual bases. A vector-space adjoint instead uses Gram corrections outside orthonormal bases.

Rule 84

Finite-dimensional hypotheses are essential to bijection implications and inverse theorems. State the sequence or function domain before using an infinite-dimensional counterexample.

29. Interactive coordinate laboratory

The stored walkthroughs above use distinct geometric, coefficient-flow, matrix-space, and coordinate-pipeline models. All start paused. Controls expose individual exact checkpoints and comparisons; a moving shape is never treated as a proof. The laboratory below lets you change an operator and two bases, independently checks both computational paths, and displays the physical input and output separately from their coordinates.

Use two-by-two integer matrices, rows separated by semicolons, entries separated by commas, and values from minus ten through ten. Both basis matrices must be invertible. All computations use exact rational arithmetic. Invalid input preserves the preceding valid result.

30. References and reading boundaries

  • Oxford University — M1 Linear Algebra I, Andrew Wathen, 2022–23. Written lecture notes, native PDF pages 53–67. Definitions, basis extension, rank–nullity, matrix representations, composition, coordinate changes, and similarity. The lecturer attribution is a course attribution, not a claim of credited PDF authorship.
  • MIT — 18.06SC Linear Algebra, Gilbert Strang, Fall 2011. Linear transformations and their matrices, all four teaching pages plus both exercises and their two teaching solution pages. Change of basis and image compression, all three teaching pages. License pages were separately identified.
  • Stanford University — EE263, Stephen Boyd, Autumn 2007–08, Lecture 3. Linear algebra review, native PDF pages 5–13. Kernel, attainable outputs, inverses, rank, and change of coordinates.
  • University of California, Berkeley — Math 54, Alexander Paulin, Spring 2018. Vector Spaces and Linear Transformations and Bases and Coordinate Systems. All eight scanned pages were read visually; native scans distinguish ambiguous subscripts and a repeated coordinate label.
  • Carnegie Mellon University — 21-241, William Gunther, Summer I 2014, Day 24. Written notes, all four pages. Additional comparison only; the source audit identifies incorrect independence, polynomial-space, and nonlinearity statements.
  • Iranian examination archive. Phd-Exam-CSE examination repository. Included items carry immutable source commits, native page numbers, and independently derived answers.

No claim of guaranteed performance on all unseen questions is made. The audit records the selected scope, exact reading, independently checked cases, source corrections, and remaining boundaries.
